titre: India's Parliament Can Amend Everything Except the Essentials
accroche: In 1973, India's Supreme Court rules that amending the Constitution through the proper procedure is not enough: its basic structure remains out of reach.
contenu_vulgarise:
February 1970, Kasaragod district, Kerala. Swami Kesavananda Bharati, head of the Hindu monastery of Edneer, the Edneer Matha, challenges in court the measures Kerala has taken, under two land reform laws, to restrict the management of his institution's property. The jurist Nanabhoy Palkhivala persuades him to base his petition on Article 26, which protects the right of a religious institution to manage its property without interference. The case, minor in appearance, will become the vehicle for a much broader question: how far can India's Parliament go in changing its own Constitution?

## A question already settled twice, in opposite ways

Since independence, the Supreme Court had given two opposite answers. An earlier decision had held that Parliament could amend every part of the Constitution, fundamental rights included. On February 27, 1967, in the Golak Nath case, eleven judges had held the opposite, by six votes to five: fundamental rights could be neither reduced nor abolished through the amendment procedure of Article 368. Parliament had replied with the Twenty-fourth Amendment, in force on November 5, 1971, which reaffirmed its power to modify any provision of the Constitution, fundamental rights included.

It is in this context that thirteen judges, the largest bench ever assembled by India's Supreme Court, hear the Kesavananda Bharati case over sixty-eight days of hearings, from October 31, 1972, to March 23, 1973.

## Seven hundred pages, eleven opinions, and a disputed majority

On April 24, 1973, the Court rules: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, fundamental rights included, but not its “basic structure.”

The judgment runs to eleven separate opinions and about seven hundred pages, and the seven-of-thirteen majority is not a simple matter to read. A statement summarizing the majority's position is signed by only nine of the thirteen judges, including the Chief Justice, S. M. Sikri. His term ends on April 25, the day after the ruling. Four judges (Ray, Mathew, Beg, and Dwivedi) did not sign it. A 2017 column in Bar & Bench also points out that seven judges use the expression “basic structure” but differ on what it covers, and asks whether one can then speak of a majority judgment at all. The basic structure doctrine thus rests on a ruling whose majority, on the precise content of the doctrine, is a matter of debate.

Nine of them sign the statement summarizing the majority's position; four judges (Ray, Mathew, Beg, and Dwivedi) did not sign it.

carte.punch: Thirteen judges, eleven opinions, and a 7-to-6 majority whose content is debated.
carte.idee: In 1973, India's Supreme Court rules that Parliament can amend the Constitution, fundamental rights included, except its “basic structure.” The statement summarizing the majority's position was signed by only nine of the thirteen judges.

quiz.question: What does India's Supreme Court rule in the Kesavananda Bharati case, in 1973?
choix: That fundamental rights can never be amended, unlike the rest of the Constitution.
That only the Supreme Court, not Parliament, has the power to modify the Constitution.
That Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, fundamental rights included, but not its basic structure.
That Parliament can amend the Constitution only with the unanimous consent of all Indian states.
quiz.explication: The ruling reverses Golak Nath (1967), which had barred changes to fundamental rights: Kesavananda Bharati allows their amendment, but not the destruction of the Constitution's basic structure.

choix: An election dispute between two Indian political parties
A complaint filed by a group of journalists censored by the government
A monastery head's challenge to land reform measures limiting the management of his property
A commercial dispute between two Indian companies
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Swami Kesavananda Bharati, head of the Hindu monastery of Edneer in Kerala, challenges measures taken under land reform laws that restrict the management of his institution's property.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did India's Supreme Court hold in the Golak Nath case, in 1967, before being partly contradicted by Kesavananda Bharati?
choix: That Parliament's amending power was entirely unlimited
That only the Supreme Court could propose constitutional amendments
That the Indian Constitution could never be amended
That fundamental rights were beyond the reach of Parliament's amending power
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On February 27, 1967, in the Golak Nath case, the Court had held the opposite of an earlier decision: fundamental rights were beyond the reach of the amendment procedure of Article 368.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many judges sat in the Kesavananda Bharati case, and how many days of hearings did it take?
choix: Five judges, over twelve days of hearings
Thirteen judges, over sixty-eight days of hearings
Twenty-one judges, over one hundred days of hearings
Nine judges, over thirty days of hearings
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Thirteen judges, the largest bench ever assembled by the Court, hear the case over sixty-eight days, from October 31, 1972, to March 23, 1973.
